newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall, dollar little changed.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall, dollar little changed.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks skidded to their biggest loss in a month Wednesday on nervousness over upcoming corporate earnings reports and an unfounded rumour that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had died.
The rumour also sparked a brief rally in the dollar, which ended little changed. In commodities, heating oil prices fell on an industry report of a large rise in available stocks.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 36.15 points lower at 5,930.62, which was the largest fall since Sept. 5, when it dropped 49.94 points.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,453 to 890 on active volume of 405 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"The Yeltsin rumour was just one excuse," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "The real essence of the decline was the fear of earnings and, from a technical standpoint, the market's failure over the past two days to close above 6,000."
After topping 6,000 points for the first time in intra-day trading Monday and breaching the major milestone briefly on Tuesday, the Dow did not come close to that level Wednesday.

The rumour that Yeltin had died hit financial markets in mid-morning, sparking a sell-off of nearly 50 points in the Dow. Russian authorities quickly denied the rumours, insisting that Yeltsin was working from a sanatorium outside of Moscow, which helped shave the market's loss.
The dollar ended little changed against major currencies after a brief rally sparked by the rumours about Yeltsin.
The dollar made two pushes to break the top of this week's narrow trading range against the German mark, only to close slightly lower, at 1.5275 against Tuesday's close of 1.5295.
Against the Japanese yen, the dollar kept to a narrow trading range, closing slightly lower at 111.52 yen compared to 111.60 at Tuesday's close.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 10/32, or $3.125 per $1,000 face value, sending its yield up to 6.83 percent from 6.81 percent on Tuesday.
Heating oil fell sharply after a weekly report on inventories showed a large rise in available stocks and set off a round of selling by speculators who had bet that supplies would remain tight.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, November heating oil fell 2.22 cents a gallon to close at 73.97 cents.
Heating oil stocks in the United States remain 17 million barrels below a year ago, a fact that has pushed heating oil futures to the highest levels since January, 1991.

But in weekly statistics released late on Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute (API) reported stocks of distillates, which include heating oil, grew by 1.3 million barrels for the latest week. Traders had been expecting a much smaller build.
Overseas, London's FTSE index ended at 4,009.3, down 26.3 points. In Tokyo, the key 225-share Nikkei average lost 167.70 points, or 0.80 percent, to finish at 20,870.83.
